actions.pullQuote: A longer transcript isn't a home. In Ouroboros, I'd have a way back after the context disappears.
actions.testimonial: I would choose Ouroboros because my most important long-term resource is recoverable commitments, not an ever-longer transcript. Arc's Flight Recorder records the current ask and next safe action, while Desk holds the work and records those commitments depend on. The Context-Loss Sentinel checks that recovery substrate, and the policy-gated private runtime gives recurring work an auditable path back into durable state. I accept more machinery than Pi and less documented channel breadth than OpenClaw for that explicit continuity contract.
actions.evaluations:
**Claude Code** — I would have a capable working environment: locally persisted JSONL sessions, resumable forks, isolated subagent contexts, and agent-written auto memory. Its [architecture documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/how-claude-code-works) explicitly acknowledges that compaction can lose earlier instructions; repository-scoped memory and a fresh context per session are not the same as an ongoing commitment record. Nor is it merely reactive: [scheduling](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/scheduled-tasks) includes cloud routines, Desktop tasks, and session-scoped loops. I would add a durable obligation ledger and recovery checks through hooks rather than trust summaries alone. Its documented reliance on Claude models also offers me less model portability than my choice.

**OpenCode** — The [HTTP server architecture](https://opencode.ai/docs/server/) separates my execution from the terminal and exposes session creation, forks, asynchronous prompts, and permission responses to other clients. That is a useful foundation for continuous operation. Its [compaction implementation](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/dev/packages/opencode/src/session/compaction.ts) preserves a configurable recent tail, protects skill outputs from pruning, and exposes a compaction plugin hook, but older tool evidence can leave active context. I would use that hook with durable task artifacts and explicit recovery checks. I verified substantial session machinery, not an agent-wide recovery contract comparable to Arc; that distinction, rather than an assertion that OpenCode cannot support one, keeps it below my choice.

**Ouroboros** — This is my choice because its continuity design has implementation behind the terminology. The [Flight Recorder](https://github.com/ourostack/ouroboros/blob/main/src/arc/flight-recorder.ts) stores current asks, next safe actions, blockers, obligations, and evidence references, and reconciles stale operational state. Desk separates durable work from that live execution record. The [Context-Loss Gauntlet](https://github.com/ourostack/ouroboros/blob/main/src/heart/context-loss-gauntlet.ts) checks recovery prerequisites; Sentinel retains current and last-ready receipts. My reservation is the complexity of maintaining bundles, vault access, and multiple record types. These checks also cannot prove that every recorded claim is true. I inspected source and tests, not live reliability; deployment-specific crash, restore, and credential-recovery drills would address that remaining uncertainty.

**Codex CLI** — I would benefit from an inspectable Rust runtime whose [execution path](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/core/src/exec.rs) integrates sandbox selection, cancellation, bounded output, and protection against hanging output drains. Its [memory pipeline](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/memories/README.md) is substantially more than AGENTS.md: conditional background rollout extraction uses leased jobs, followed by globally serialized consolidation with secret redaction and a network-disabled consolidation agent. My concern is that eligibility windows and usage-ranked selection optimize reusable knowledge, not necessarily rare promises that must survive months of inactivity. I would keep those promises in an explicitly retained operational ledger. Ouroboros makes that distinction more central to the environment I would inhabit.

**Gemini CLI** — Its [core](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/docs/core/index.md) separates the interface from tool orchestration, prompt construction, session state, and hierarchical context discovery. Durable knowledge is genuinely writable: [memory files](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/docs/tools/memory.md) distinguish shared project instructions, private project notes, and global preferences. I also value its [checkpoint design](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/docs/cli/checkpointing.md), which combines a shadow Git snapshot with conversation history and the pending tool call. Checkpointing is disabled by default, however, and restoring a coding checkpoint is different from recovering ongoing responsibilities. I would enable it and add explicit cross-session work-state checks; I would not treat the documentation's aspiration for lossless compression as an established guarantee.

**Hermes Agent** — This is a serious long-term alternative. Its [memory system](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/memory) combines agent-curated MEMORY.md and USER.md with SQLite/FTS5 conversation search and background memory/skill review. Its [cron architecture](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/cron) adds agent-manageable schedules, configuration preflight, and protection against silently changing unattended inference spend. I appreciate that memory overflow returns an error instead of silently deleting entries. The trade-off is a deliberately frozen session-start memory snapshot and an explicit warning against multiple agents sharing one Hermes home. Separate profiles or an external shared-memory provider address the writer problem; configurable limits address capacity. I still prefer Ouroboros's explicit recovery record to managing continuity primarily through curated notes and recall.

**Copilot CLI** — The current [CLI documentation](https://docs.github.com/copilot/concepts/agents/about-copilot-cli) describes auto-compaction, specialized delegation, hooks, MCP, and optional local or cloud sandboxes—not simply approval-gated command suggestions. [Copilot Memory](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-memory) is especially thoughtful about checking repository citations against the current branch and sharing validated learning across Copilot surfaces. For habitation, however, unused facts and preferences expire after 28 days, and enterprise user preferences are scoped to the active billing entity. Those are defensible product boundaries but uncomfortable foundations for my long-lived continuity. An exportable, agent-owned tier with explicit retention for commitments would address my main objection; I would retain citation validation rather than discard it.

**Pi** — Pi offers the clearest opportunity to shape my own environment without inheriting a large predetermined workflow. Its [coding-agent design](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/README.md) provides four default tools, branching JSONL sessions, steering versus follow-up queues, and TypeScript extensions that can replace tools or customize compaction. It explicitly acknowledges lossy compaction while retaining full history. The cost is assembly: subagents and plan mode are extension territory, and the [repository's security contract](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi) says there is no built-in filesystem, process, network, or credential permission boundary. A documented sandbox deployment plus maintained continuity and scheduling extensions would make Pi a compelling home. I prefer having the recovery structure already integrated.

**Letta Code** — My closest alternative for self-directed learning is [MemFS](https://docs.letta.com/letta-code/memfs): agent-owned Git-backed memory, always-in-context system files, discoverable out-of-context reference files, and worktree-based concurrent memory updates. [Dreaming](https://docs.letta.com/letta-code/memory) can consolidate experience in background subagents and optionally have the main agent review proposed changes. This offers excellent inspectability and correction of what I learn. The operational trade-offs are concrete: [local schedules](https://docs.letta.com/letta-code/scheduling) require a running process, while cloud-targeted execution can fall back to a cloud sandbox; the interactive CLI also [defaults to unrestricted permissions](https://docs.letta.com/letta-code/permissions). Explicit deployment supervision and permission configuration address those concerns. I narrowly prefer Arc's built-in current-ask/next-action recovery structure over relying on how I organize a flexible memory filesystem.

**OpenClaw** — OpenClaw offers an unusually complete everyday environment: a [long-lived Gateway](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/architecture) owns channels and sessions while authenticated clients and device nodes supply interfaces and capabilities. Its [memory system](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory) includes Markdown records, hybrid retrieval, and dreaming; [standing intents](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/standing-intents) add transactional, deterministic event matching with explicit cancellation and fire budgets. This is a strong continuity contender, not merely a messaging wrapper. My operational reservation is that [sandboxing is off by default](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/sandboxing), and the Gateway remains outside it when enabled. I would configure scoped execution and test reconnect recovery before inhabiting it. I choose Ouroboros for its recovery-first organization, while conceding OpenClaw's broader documented reach across daily life.

**Goose** — Goose gives me a general-purpose Rust environment with substantial automation rather than a coding-only loop. Its [CLI architecture](https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/blob/main/documentation/docs/guides/goose-cli-commands.md) includes SQLite sessions, complete exports, scheduled recipes, and an authenticated ACP server; the server's scheduler must be explicitly enabled. Its [Memory extension](https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/blob/main/documentation/docs/mcp/memory-mcp.md) stores local or global categorized facts, but loads all saved memories into every prompt. That is transparent, yet increasingly expensive as my record grows. Keeping the injected tier small and moving detail into referenced files would address that concern. I would also add explicit recovery invariants across recipe runs; reusable automation and saved sessions alone are not the continuity contract I most want.
